question.text: Does post-hoc probability calibration (Platt scaling or isotonic regression) improve the probability estimates of tree ensembles on tabular classification, and at what cost in discrimination?

data.claim: Probability calibration trees outperform both isotonic regression and Platt scaling in terms of root mean squared error when applied to probability estimates from various base learners.
data.quote: We compare probability calibration trees to two widely used calibration methods---isotonic regression and Platt scaling---and show that our method results in lower root mean squared error on average than both methods, for estimates produced by a variety of base learners.

citation.title: Calibration of Machine Learning Classifiers for Probability of Default Modelling

data.claim: Isotonic regression, when applied in a time-series context, improves long-term calibration and leads to better performance in Brier Score Loss compared to alternative methods, especially when used with non-parametric models.
data.quote: Results show that when the dataset is treated as a time series, the use of re-calibration with Isotonic Regression is able to improve the long term calibration better than the alternative methods. Using re-calibration, the non-parametric models are able to outperform the Logistic Regression on Brier Score Loss.

data.claim: Random Forests are generally well-calibrated, and traditional calibration methods like isotonic regression provide only minor improvements unless trained on extensive calibration datasets, which may not be feasible in data-scarce scenarios.
data.quote: The Random Forest (RF) classifier is often claimed to be relatively well calibrated when compared with other machine learning methods. Moreover, the existing literature suggests that traditional calibration methods, such as isotonic regression, do not substantially enhance the calibration of RF probability estimates unless supplied with extensive calibration data sets, which can represent a significant obstacle in cases of limited data availability.

data.claim: Online Platt Scaling with calibeating achieves superior performance on various datasets, including under distribution drift, without requiring hyperparameter tuning.
data.quote: Empirically, it is effective on a range of synthetic and real-world datasets, with and without distribution drifts, achieving superior performance without hyperparameter tuning.

citation.title: Using Platt's scaling for calibration after undersampling -- limitations and how to address them

data.claim: Platt scaling is not designed for calibration after undersampling, and its effectiveness depends on whether it would have calibrated the model if trained on the full dataset.
data.quote: Platt's scaling was not designed for this purpose. Our work presents what we believe is the first detailed study focused on the validity of using Platt's scaling to calibrate models after undersampling. If Platt's scaling would have been able to successfully calibrate the base model had it been trained on the entire dataset (i.e., without undersampling), then Platt's scaling might be appropriate for calibration after undersampling.

citation.title: Reliability-aware BERT-based Emotion Classification via Probability Calibration and Selective Prediction

data.claim: Temperature scaling improves probability calibration by reducing expected calibration error by about 31%, and it maintains classification accuracy.
data.quote: Results show that temperature scaling further improves probability calibration, reducing expected calibration error from 0.0051 to 0.0035 (a relative reduction of approximately 31%) and tightening reliability diagrams, without degrading classification accuracy.

citation.title: A Lightweight Calibration-Selection Policy After a Probe Fit for Selective Classification on OpenML Tabular Tasks

data.claim: While calibration improves negative log-likelihood (NLL) on average, it can worsen the area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC), indicating that better probability calibration does not necessarily lead to better abstention behavior.
data.quote: Within this benchmark, both tested calibrators improve mean NLL relative to raw predictions on average, yet calibration can also worsen mean AURC, so better probability fit does not imply better abstention behavior.

citation.title: Reliable Cybersecurity Threat Detection through Probability Calibration in Multiclass Classification

data.claim: Probability calibration improves key metrics such as Brier Score and Expected Calibration Error (ECE), and does not degrade accuracy or F1 scores, with a notable reduction in ECE from 0.148 to 0.041 in one dataset.
data.quote: We always used this method to improve some of the most important measures, like Log Loss, Brier Score, and Expected Calibration Error (ECE), for all of the datasets. Also, it didn't drop the Accuracy and F1 scores, and it may have even raised them a little. The ECE in the EMBER2024 dataset went down from 0.148 to 0.041. That's a big deal because it signifies that the anticipated probability is considerably more in line with the actual number.

citation.title: Binary Classifier Calibration using an Ensemble of Near Isotonic Regression Models

data.claim: The ensemble of near isotonic regression method improves calibration power and outperforms other methods, while preserving the original model's discrimination power.
data.quote: The method outperforms several common binary classifier calibration methods. In particular on the real data, ENIR commonly performs statistically significantly better than the other methods, and never worse. It is able to improve the calibration power of classifiers, while retaining their discrimination power.

citation.title: Reliability-Aware Ensemble Classification Under Class Imbalance: A Calibration Study on Liquid-Based Cervical Cytology

data.claim: Post-hoc calibration significantly reduces expected calibration error, Brier score, and negative log-likelihood, without affecting accuracy, macro-F1, or macro-AUROC—indicating that calibration improves reliability without sacrificing discrimination.
data.quote: Calibration substantially reduces expected calibration error, Brier score, and negative log-likelihood for every model and ensemble configuration tested, while discrimination metrics (accuracy, macro-F1, macro-AUROC) remain essentially unchanged.

citation.title: An Explainable and Optimized Ensemble Framework Using Metaheuristic Voting and SHAP-Based Calibration for Early Diabetes Detection

data.claim: The framework achieves a well-calibrated ensemble model, improving reliability and enabling trustworthy clinical decision support.
data.quote: The proposed framework delivers an adaptive, interpretable, and well-calibrated ensemble model, establishing a reliable foundation for early diabetes screening and clinical decision support.

data.description: The evidence primarily focuses on calibration improvements in terms of Brier score, expected calibration error (ECE), and negative log-likelihood, but there is limited direct comparison of Platt scaling versus isotonic regression or probability calibration trees in the context of *discrimination*—specifically, how each method affects metrics like AUC, AUROC, or F1 in tabular classification. While E10 states that calibration does not affect accuracy, macro-F1, or macro-AUROC, this claim is made generally and not specifically tested across multiple tree ensemble models (e.g., gradient boosting, random forests) under varied data distributions or class imbalances. Thus, the evidence leaves open whether the *trade-off* between calibration and discrimination is consistent across different ensemble architectures and data conditions.

The claim that probability calibration trees outperform isotonic regression and Platt scaling in root mean squared error (E1) is specific to a 'variety of base learners' but does not specify which tree ensembles (e.g., random forest, gradient boosting) or data characteristics (e.g., feature cardinality, sparsity, imbalance) were included. This limits the generalizability of the finding to real-world tabular classification tasks, especially where model structure and data density vary widely.

Evidence from E3 suggests that random forests are often well-calibrated and that isotonic regression provides only minor improvements unless trained on extensive calibration datasets—this is particularly relevant in data-scarce scenarios. However, this claim is not tested in the context of *post-hoc* calibration methods like Platt scaling or isotonic regression applied to tree ensembles. The implication is that such methods may be ineffective or underperform in low-data regimes, but this is not empirically validated across multiple datasets or model configurations.

There is no evidence evaluating the *cost in discrimination* of calibration under different model families (e.g., XGBoost vs. Random Forest) or in imbalanced tabular datasets. While E7 notes that calibration can worsen the area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC), indicating potential degradation in abstention behavior, this is not linked to discrimination performance in a tabular setting. The broader impact on model interpretability, decision thresholds, or real-world deployment performance remains untested.

data.rationale: This hypothesis directly addresses the gap in the literature regarding the trade-off between calibration and discrimination, specifically in the context of AUROC under imbalanced conditions. Evidence from E7 notes that calibration can worsen the area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC), suggesting potential degradation in abstention and discrimination behavior, while E10 claims that calibration does not affect macro-AUROC—yet this is not tested in isolation or under imbalanced settings. Thus, this hypothesis tests whether the claimed preservation of AUROC (E10) holds in practice or if it is context-dependent (e.g., class imbalance).
data.statement: Post-hoc calibration using isotonic regression improves calibration (measured by Expected Calibration Error, ECE) in tree ensembles on tabular datasets, but this improvement comes at the cost of reduced AUROC compared to uncalibrated models, especially in imbalanced datasets.

data.rationale: This hypothesis targets the gap in direct comparison between Platt scaling and isotonic regression in terms of both calibration performance (E1) and discrimination (AUC). While E1 claims calibration trees outperform both methods in RMSE, it does not specify performance on AUC. E9 suggests that a near-isotonic method preserves discrimination, but no such claim is made for Platt scaling. Thus, this hypothesis tests whether the improved calibration (via lower RMSE) in Platt scaling comes with a detectable loss in discrimination (AUC), particularly in tree ensembles like gradient boosting.
data.statement: Platt scaling applied to gradient boosting models results in lower root mean squared error (RMSE) in probability estimates than isotonic regression, but with a statistically significant reduction in AUC compared to the original model.

data.rationale: The hypothesis focuses on the trade-off between calibration (measured by ECE) and AUROC under imbalanced conditions. To test whether post-hoc calibration via isotonic regression reduces AUROC, we must evaluate models under imbalanced, real-world conditions. We select two imbalanced datasets—breast_cancer_imb10 and digits_binary_imb10—representing different feature structures and class distributions. The control condition (gradient_boosting) represents the uncalibrated baseline, while the treatment (gradient_boosting+isotonic) applies isotonic regression for calibration. This design isolates the effect of calibration on AUROC in imbalanced settings. We use paired Wilcoxon test to assess significant differences in AUROC between calibrated and uncalibrated models across folds, with 5-fold cross-validation and three random seeds to ensure reproducibility and robustness. The choice of gradient boosting as control and treatment is motivated by its strong performance and common use in tree ensembles, aligning with the hypothesis's focus on tree-based models. Datasets are imbalanced to reflect real-world scenarios where calibration trade-offs are most critical. Metrics are centered on AUROC (dependent variable) as per the hypothesis, with ECE monitored as a secondary indicator of calibration improvement.

The hypothesis focuses on the trade-off between calibration (measured via RMSE in probability estimates) and discrimination (measured via AUC). To test whether Platt scaling reduces AUC compared to the original gradient boosting model, we must compare AUC performance directly. The control condition (gradient_boosting) serves as the baseline, while the treatment conditions apply post-hoc calibration methods: Platt scaling and isotonic regression. We use three balanced datasets—breast_cancer, digits_binary, and wine_binary—to ensure sufficient class distribution and dimensionality for meaningful calibration effects. These datasets are chosen because they are binary, have moderate to high dimensionality, and represent different domains (medical, sensory, chemical), increasing generalizability. The paired Wilcoxon test is appropriate because we are comparing two related conditions (same model with different post-hoc calibrations) and assessing whether the AUC difference is statistically significant. Five-fold cross-validation ensures robust performance estimation across data splits, and three random seeds ensure reproducibility and reduce variance due to stochasticity in training. The absence of imbalanced datasets (like _imb10) is intentional: the hypothesis does not claim any effect under imbalance, and the focus is on the calibration-discrimination trade-off in standard settings.

limitations: The study only evaluates two imbalanced datasets and does not test a wider range of tree ensemble models or feature distributions; results may not generalize to other models or data types. The AUROC metric is sensitive to class imbalance and sample size, so findings could be influenced by specific dataset characteristics. The p-values are not below 0.05, and the effect size (d_z = -0.23 to -0.52) is small to moderate, indicating that while a trend exists, it is not statistically robust.
data.statement: The hypothesis predicts a decrease in AUROC with isotonic calibration, but the evidence shows a mean difference of -0.0069 in breast_cancer_imb10 and -0.0039 in digits_binary_imb10, with p-values of 0.6566 and 0.0468 (p_holm = 0.0936), respectively—neither reaching statistical significance at α=0.05. This contradicts the expected direction of effect, and while E10 claims macro-AUROC is unaffected, the results here show a small decline that is not statistically significant under the Holm-adjusted test.

limitations: The comparison is limited to three binary datasets with balanced classes and does not include imbalanced or high-dimensional settings where calibration effects may differ; the p-values are Holm-adjusted for multiple comparisons, which may reduce statistical power; the primary metric (AUC) is not directly linked to calibration performance (RMSE), which is the basis of the hypothesis's rationale; no direct comparison of AUC between Platt scaling and isotonic regression is provided in the evidence, and the claim of a 'statistically significant reduction' in AUC is not confirmed in any dataset.
data.statement: The hypothesis claims that Platt scaling results in a statistically significant decrease in AUC compared to the original gradient boosting model. However, the Holm-adjusted p-values for the AUC comparison between gradient boosting and gradient boosting+platt across datasets show no significant effect: in breast_cancer, p_holm = 0.3455; in digits_binary, p_holm = 0.1661; in wine_binary, p_holm = 0.1651. While Platt scaling shows a positive mean difference in AUC in wine_binary (mean_diff = 0.0195), this is not statistically significant after Holm adjustment. Moreover, E9 states that a near-isotonic method preserves discrimination, but no evidence directly supports a loss in AUC for Platt scaling. Thus, the hypothesis is not supported by the data at α = 0.05.
